title: Anatomy of Medical School
summary:
Cover image by Tara Winstead

By Althea Need Kaminske

I work as a Medical Education Learning Specialist (MELS) at a large medical school in the US. My job is to take the science of learning and apply it to a very specific educational environment: undergraduate medical education. While a fair bit of that involves breaking down the science of learning, it also requires understanding the context in which the learning is taking place. In this post I want to explain the basic structure of medical school and licensing exams. This may be of interest to any incoming or aspiring medical students (particularly within the US since I will focus on the US medical school system), MELS colleagues, or anyone who knows someone in medical school and is curious about what it’s like.

Medical school, as a pre-professional school that trains students for the responsibility of patient care, presents some unique challenges. Medical students are future physicians, and are expected to be knowledgeable in both a wide array of medical knowledge as well as clinical best practices. Training medical students becomes more challenging each year as the amount of medical knowledge only ever increases. Upon graduation, a medical doctor is a generalist - they must possess a broad skill set, ready to enter into a number of specialties. Medical schools can vary widely in how they approach the education and training of medical students, though there are some notable similarities in medical schools around the world. They tend to have similar phases of training: a pre-clinical phase that focuses on medical knowledge, a clinical phase that focuses on exposure to clinical practice in a core set of specialties, and a career-exploration phase where students gain clinical experience in specialties that they want to focus on. Training in medical school also includes a focus on licensure exams specific to the country one will be practicing in. Finally, both clinical skills and medical knowledge are assessed throughout. 

Allopathic vs Osteopathic

Medical schools within the U.S. can vary as to whether they offer allopathic or osteopathic training. Allopathic medicine focuses on the diagnosis and treatment of diseases and allopathic schools grant Medical Doctorates (M.D.s). Osteopathic places a greater emphasis on holistic medicine, treating the body as an interconnected whole, and osteopathic schools grant Doctorates of Osteopathic Medicine (D.O.s). Within the U.S. about 70% of medical students are working toards an M.D. and 30% are working towards a D.O. (https://www.aacom.org/become-a-doctor/about-osteopathic-medicine/quick-facts). While there are differences between the two traditions of medical training, notably the emphasis on physical manipulation within osteopathic programs, the structure of these medical programs has converged over time. Both are comprised of pre-clinical coursework, core clinical training, and career-exploration.


Board Exams

Given the responsibility of a medical doctor, students must pass licensure exams in addition to regular course requirements. In the U.S. the National Board of Medical Examiners (NBME) delivers the United States Medical Licensing Exam (USMLE) in a series of three “steps”: Step 1, Step 2, and Step 3. Similarly, the National Board of Osteopathic Medical Examiners (NOBME) delivers the Comprehensive Osteopathic Medical Licensing Examination (COMLEX) in a series of three levels: Level 1, Level 2, and Level 3. Medical schools vary as to when students are required to take and pass the Step exams. Students may graduate with an MD, or DO,  having met the requirements of their degree program, but are not able to practice as a licensed physician until they have passed all three licensure exams. Given the importance of licensing exams, it is difficult to discuss learning in medical school without addressing how to prepare for these major exams.

QBanks

The extraordinary volume of information and the high-stakes nature of the board exams has led to an entire industry of test-preparation tools. While there are a few different types of study tools marketed towards medical schools, the biggest ones are question banks (QBanks). Selection and use of QBanks is one of the most prominent features of any board exam prep. These tools - UWorld, Amboss, or TrueLearn - to name a few, leverage the use of retrieval and spaced practice to improve understanding and retention of material. In preparation for board exams, students frequently exhaust these QBanks, which have thousands of questions in them. Something that surprised me as I started my role as a MELS, was how ubiquitous these QBanks are and how students were already very familiar with the concept of retrieval practice (I recently wrote about this with some other cognitive psychologist MELS!). 

Undergraduate, Graduate, and Continuing Medical Education

As I mentioned above, I work primarily in undergraduate medical education. As a PhD, this was initially confusing for me. I completed my undergraduate training at university alongside pre-med students. I then went on to graduate school at the same time that some of my classmates went on to medical school. In medical education, undergraduate medical education, or UME, is distinguished from graduate medical education (GME). UME refers to schooling prior to obtaining an M.D. or O.D., and GME refers to training as a resident within a specialty. Thus, medical students complete general undergraduate education then go into medical school where they complete undergraduate medical education. 

Within UME, medical students must take and pass the first 2 out of 3 board exams to be able to practice as a licensed doctor. Once in a specialty specific residency program (e.g., family medicine, general surgery, pediatrics, etc.) they are expected to take the third exam to be fully licensed as a general practitioner. At this GME level they are also in training to take their specialty-specific board exam. Each specialty oversees and administers their own standards for within their discipline, and residents within GME must take and pass those exams as well. 

Because of the ever-growing body of medical knowledge, and fast-evolving best-practices, all practicing physicians must maintain active certification within their specialty. This phase of medical education is called Continuing Medical Education (CME). All physicians must continue with CME throughout their career in order to remain certified within their specialty. While the nature and pace of these exams is very different from UME (medical students take A LOT of exams), anyone going into medicine needs to be able to take and pass board exams as part of their professional skill set.


Given the constant need for learning new information and the expectation to demonstrate that knowledge on exams, a growing professional field within medical education is Medical Education Learning Specialists (MELS). MELS help learners (whether at the UME, GME, or CME level) to adjust their study strategies and test taking strategies in order to be as successful as possible. I view my job as helping learners to understand their learning in the context of whatever they are going through. Oftentimes, study strategies developed outside of the context of medical education are not successful within medical education. The high volume of content, high-stakes nature of the exams, and increasing and changing professional responsibilities make studying and passing exams markedly different within medication education compared to university, as well as different across UME, GME, and CME.

summary: A surprising new discovery suggests that fear may cause the brain to blur the line between danger and safety rather than distinguish them more clearly. title: Scientists discover mysterious “lonely” brain waves linked to memory loss
summary: Scientists have uncovered a surprising link between Alzheimer’s-related protein buildup, disrupted brain waves during deep sleep, and fading memory. title: Scientists discover why chronic back pain feels so personal

title: Six Factors That Support Mental Health for Black Youth
summary:
On a summer day at UC Berkeley, four teenagers jostled at a whiteboard, vying to write down their solutions to an important public health concern. They were having fun even as they took on a heavy task: helping researchers design programs to reduce the skyrocketing suicide rate among Black youth. 

In the United States, deaths by suicide have been surging among Black kids and teens for decades. For those between 10 and 17 years of age, the suicide rate rose 144% from 2007 to 2020. What’s more, Black boys die by suicide more than twice as frequently as Black girls, although the suicide rate for Black girls increased by 182% between 2001 and 2017.

As the teenagers brainstormed, Jasmin Brooks Stephens, a Berkeley assistant professor of psychology, watched nearby. The moment was a highlight in research she was conducting with the Homeless Children’s Network on improving mental health outcomes for Black youth. Brooks Stephens believed that teens themselves have meaningful ideas to share, and she had worked for eight weeks with these particular teenagers, who were part of the network’s Jabali Youth Advocacy organization, culminating in their trip to campus.

“One of the most exciting things was seeing them all jump up and say, ‘Wait, we can make a program for making us feel better? We have the power to do that?’” Brooks Stephens recalled. “Seeing them find and discover that sense of agency in themselves—that was invaluable to me.” It also was one of the few times any of the teens had visited a college campus, she said, an added bonus. In future work, Brooks Stephens plans to translate the results of her study for clinicians and policymakers who are trying to improve suicide prevention for Black youth. 

The ongoing project is just one example of how Brooks Stephens is working to address rising suicide rates among Black youth by engaging them in participatory research—an unusual and hopeful approach in suicide prevention studies. “This summer I had the incredible opportunity to work alongside young people to design a program that would help other young people want to live,” she said. “Rather than waiting until a young person is already in crisis, I’m interested in understanding what helps youth thrive—what gives them hope and a sense of possibility and helps them recognize the brilliance they have inside them.”

A pathway to hope in the face of racism

Despite the growing crisis among Black youth, suicide rates are dropping for adolescents in the U.S. overall. Brooks Stephens finds these statistics revealing: “To me, that suggests that the approaches we have relied on have not adequately addressed the conditions driving suicide risk in Black communities,” she said. 

It’s easy to talk about structural racism as an abstract concept, or personal encounters with racists as disturbing but bounded moments. But grappling with racism heavily impacts Black youth and increases their suicide risk, according to a 2023 report from the Johns Hopkins Bloomberg School of Public Health. Indeed, Brooks Stephens has published work documenting how racial discrimination and the COVID-19 pandemic, which disproportionately harmed Black Americans, together worsened suicide risk for Black young adults. 

Brooks Stephens’s work is informed by both her research and her own experience of how race can shape young people’s sense of self. “I became aware very early on that Black children are often navigating expectations about who they are supposed to be before they have even had the opportunity to figure out who they are for themselves,” she said. “That has stayed with me—the importance of creating space for Black young people to define themselves, recognize their strengths, and imagine who they want to become.” At the same time, she saw how the stigma surrounding mental health could make it harder for Black youth and families to seek support, even as racism and other chronic stressors were impacting their well-being. 

When she took an African American psychology class as an undergraduate at the University of North Carolina, Chapel Hill, with Enrique Neblett, a renowned scholar of race and health who became her mentor, Brooks Stephens saw the connection between those experiences—and found her passion. “I realized that there was an entire field devoted to understanding how racism affects mental health and how Black children come to understand themselves and their racial identity,” she said. 

Later, during her doctoral research at the University of Houston, Brooks Stephens worked with Rheeda Walker, an expert on suicide science and African American adult mental health research. Brooks Stephens noticed that there was very limited discussion about building upstream resilience in suicide prevention research—an approach that focuses on child well-being and happiness before the development of a mental health crisis. 

“We’re studying why people choose to end their life without understanding what makes people want to live,” she said. For Brooks Stephens, that realization opened up a different way of thinking about suicide prevention, one that made room for the strengths that were often absent from traditional models, such as racial identity, spirituality, family connection, belonging, or hope. 

Focusing on strengths to prevent suicide

Brooks Stephens knows she can’t single-handedly eliminate the racial traumas faced by young Black people. Nor can she end other factors that lead to higher suicide rates in her community, such as systemic injustice or poverty. Instead, she’s focusing on where she can make a difference through her research.

“While I may not be able to eradicate racism, I can help build programs that change how Black young people see themselves and their futures—programs that help them feel grounded in their identity and able to imagine a life that feels worth living,” she said. 

Brooks Stephens and her colleagues identified six positive factors that reduce suicidality among Black youth (courtesy of Jasmin Brooks Stephens).
            

As a first step, this year she and her colleagues created the Black Youth Thriving Framework for Suicide Prevention. It’s based on a literature review that identified six protective factors that can reduce suicidality among Black youth, including family support, community ties, and self-acceptance. “What we’re working to identify now are the strategies that can help cultivate those strengths in young people’s lives,” Brooks Stephens said.

Already, in a study from 2023, she and her colleagues showed that Black young adults with stronger feelings of self-acceptance are less vulnerable to depression and suicide. Likewise, she has identified mindfulness and meditation as potential tools for Black Americans in their early 20s to buffer the impulsivity that is often associated with suicide risk. 

This approach is a radical departure from the status quo. Right now, resources for preventing suicide orbit around moments of crisis, Brooks Stephens said. When a child shows signs of depression or arrives at a hospital following a suicide attempt, that’s when an intervention is often provided. Brooks Stephens wants to develop research-backed ways to prevent a child from ever getting to that troubling point in the first place. 

And, increasingly, she is asking Black young people themselves to help determine what those approaches should look like. Brooks Stephens said that the four teens with whom she worked this summer were not simply research participants; they were collaborators in imagining what suicide prevention could become.

“It’s very uplifting for me because I’m bringing underserved voices into our research and I’m designing solutions,” she said. “And those solutions are how we make kids want to live and love themselves. That’s it. It’s loving themselves, loving their life. That’s what I’m helping them discover.”

title: How Becoming a Parent Can Change Your Memories of Your Own Parents
summary:
It was around Christmas time when Emily* noticed that something was wrong. She had just welcomed her second son in September and still felt emotionally raw from the experience. Part of Emily’s postpartum planning had revolved around having her mum look after her three-year-old while she took care of the new baby. But every time she visited her parents, something in her tensed up, her mind went foggy, and instead of feeling the safety and relaxation she had been craving, she felt on edge. 

Emily sought help from me in therapy just before Christmas when she realized that the prospect of spending the holidays with her parents was making it difficult for her to sleep and the few precious hours she had between feeds were taken up with anxious rumination. She couldn’t make any sense of it. It was like a switch had flipped and the previously supportive, albeit slightly emotionally disconnected, relationship she had had with her parents was in pieces.

I work a lot with mothers and birthing people in the perinatal phase, and the change they experience in their relationship with their parents is something that comes up very frequently. Sometimes this change is positive, where they become more understanding of parents who were trying their best at the time. Sometimes it’s disorienting, like Emily’s, and the relationship seems to worsen. Either way, it’s important to meet yourself with compassion and curiosity when unexpected feelings or memories resurface during this period of your life and try not to go through this transition on your own. 

Renegotiating our childhood memories

Emily came to see me for help with anxiety and insomnia, and a few sessions into our therapy she started to talk about memories that had been appearing for her, scenes from her childhood that suddenly had taken on new meaning or had popped up out of nowhere. It was as if her memories had changed, which made Emily feel crazy and even more anxious because she felt like she couldn’t trust herself anymore.    

In the crudest terms, we tend to think of memory as a filing cabinet—a place where scenes, facts, annoying songs, and embarrassing moments are stored to be recalled, like when we try to remember what we had for dinner last week or where we went on holiday three years ago. 

When I talk about memory with my clients, they usually understand that it is not a perfect system, that it can alter over time and be very subjective. What is harder to convey is that decades of research suggest that memory is not in fact a filing cabinet or a library catalogue—it’s a construction. Every time I try to remember where we went on holiday three summers ago, my brain doesn’t retrieve but rather constructs a memory of our trip to Italy. That means that each time we recall something, that memory can change slightly or take on new meaning. Researchers Daniel L. Schacter and Donna Rose Addis found that, in fact, remembering and imagining look very similar in terms of activation in the brain.    

Why does that matter? It can help make sense of what happened to Emily and what happens to many of my clients when they become parents and their relationships with their own parents change. Some of this is explained by a shift in roles: When a child becomes a parent, the dynamic of the child-parent relationship naturally has to change, which can be difficult for both parties. Grandparents and new parents might find it challenging to adapt to who is in charge and “who knows best.” But sometimes the difficulty is more subtle, and it’s related to memory. 

When our goals change, our memories can change

Emily struggled because she had started to have visceral memories of herself at about three to five years old, even though she had never actively thought about her childhood much before. She associated that phase in her life with a feeling of paralysis that she couldn’t explain. She told me how exhausted she felt every time she left her parents’ house now, like she had been holding her breath for hours. 

Emily knew from whispered family stories that her mother had dealt with bouts of depression through much of her childhood. She also knew that her parents’ marriage hadn’t always been as placid and quiet as it was now. She had always had memories of them fighting late at night but had never thought much of it. Now she remembered her mother in tears, shouting and doors slamming. She remembered hiding under her bed.

Memory is heavily influenced by our current state of mind. Martin Conway, in his papers on autobiographical memory, explains that when we try to retrieve a memory or remember something spontaneously, we construct that memory in the moment, partly based on our current goals. If we are hungry, we might construct a memory of a cafe we saw on our walk two weeks ago. If we have a fight with our partner, we might suddenly remember all the times they disappointed us, when we usually are able to accept their imperfections. 

When Emily became a parent, her goals changed dramatically, and it changed what memories her brain predicted might be useful for her.

Emily realized that her experience of being her son’s age was one of bracing and zoning out because she had felt disconnected from her mother and scared of her father at the time. As a parent, Emily was suddenly able to attune to what it felt like for her to be three years old. Her three-year-old self did not feel safe, and she did not believe her child was safe, either. 

Conway notes that the memories we are able to construct have to be coherent with how we think of ourselves, our beliefs about ourselves, and the world and people in it. According to Conway’s theory, our brains filter, rationalize, or dismiss memories that are inconsistent with who we believe we are. 

Before Emily had children, she believed, largely unconsciously, that her childhood experiences were irrelevant to who she was and that she hadn’t really been affected by them. When she became a mum, her visceral memories of childhood fear did not match up with who she believed she was anymore. Her goals had changed from surviving and rationalizing to tuning in to and protecting her child. Her brain was telling her she had to shield her child from something that she had experienced as frightening as a child. 

Meeting our parents with compassion

Other clients of mine have found that becoming a parent had the opposite effect. They were able to look at the younger versions of their parents with more compassion and kindness, reconstructing memories through the eyes of an exhausted parent who was trying and barely coping. 

Karen and her parents had had a difficult relationship. Karen’s parents divorced when she was young, and Karen had always felt her mother had been unavailable when she was a child. She experienced a lot of anger when thinking about her childhood. She had memories of having to take on responsibilities too early, looking after her siblings, and cooking and cleaning while her mother was at work. Karen had purposefully moved away from her parents and had spent years asserting her independence. She had never wanted children because she had such strong memories of what it had been like to be a young caretaker and not being able to feel like a child. When she met her husband, she realized that creating her own family was more important to her than she had thought. 

Karen came to see me for anxiety. She was worried about losing her freedom when she became a mother, and we thought about how her childhood experiences shaped her experience now. I saw Karen for quite some time after she gave birth, and something shifted for her when she became a parent. She remembered instances of seeing her mother frazzled, rushed, and overwhelmed and how hard she had tried to find time to be there for Karen and her siblings. Karen started to realize how impossible it must have been for her mother to raise three children on her own while working. 

Karen tried to talk to her mother and learned about how ashamed she was for burdening her daughter and unsure about whether Karen wanted her in her life. To her surprise, Karen experienced her mother’s relationship with her own daughter as reparative. She could make sense of her anger and her need for freedom and see that what happened in her childhood was not something her mother had intended. 

Moving forward

For Emily, too, her experiences meant she had to rebuild the relationship with her mother and find a more honest foundation. She was able to have conversations with her about what it would have been like for Emily growing up, and, to Emily’s surprise, her mother also listened and apologized for not having checked in with her sooner. It started a healing process for Emily that involved listening to what her three-year-old self might have felt and acknowledging that she had been trying to rationalize her way out of feeling for most of her life. She had to slowly let herself experience that her parents were safe now; she decided to not rely on them for child care but let the relationship grow more slowly.  

What helped Emily was hearing her mother validate what happened to her as a child. It was something Emily would have needed when she was younger. She was also able to make new meaning of her relationship with her parents through therapy—an act of shared social construction with another human, the therapist, that fulfills some of our core needs of being heard, seen, and understood.

Karen similarly needed to feel heard by her mother. Her anger dissipated when she was able to put herself into her mother’s shoes and see that her and her mother’s experience could exist side by side. 

What can you do if parenthood is shifting your relationship with your own parents? Here are steps that I have found are helpful for my clients.  

Find support. The first step in coping with a difficult experience is to not try to go through it alone. We are social beings who need to feel understood by others. Seek out a friend or a sibling if you are struggling with feelings you do not understand. 

Meet yourself with self-compassion. When strong emotions come up, we might tell ourselves, “I’m overreacting,” “I’m too sensitive,” “I just need to get on with things and stop complaining.” Self-criticism can perpetuate a cycle in which we invalidate our experiences until they become impossible to ignore. It also won’t help to be overly critical of yourself if you believe you’ve been judging your parents too harshly, now that you have the perspective of being a parent yourself. 

Seek out conversations. If thinking back on your childhood memories brings up a perspective change on your childhood, speak to your family, your parents or siblings, and learn about how they experienced that time and you as a child. It might help you feel more compassion with your parents who may have been struggling, and can also help you understand yourself better as a person.  

Set boundaries, if needed. If memories from your childhood suddenly take on new meaning, it might be important to think about boundaries and clear rules to set with your child’s grandparents. If you felt unsafe or uncomfortable as a child, it is OK to make it clear how you expect the adults in your child’s life to behave. This can, of course, be easier said than done, and it can be useful to seek help to deal with feelings of guilt or anxiety around setting boundaries with your parents.

Seek out professional help. Remember that every experience is subjective—your version of what happened might be different from that of your siblings or your parents. That does not make it any less valid. While Emily was lucky that her mother acknowledged her experience, your family members might not always be so receptive and might be more defensive about any wrongdoing. Seeking professional help can be especially useful when you are dealing with a family system that is less likely to take responsibility or want to change. 

Becoming a parent changes your world in a thousand ways and can dramatically alter the way you look at your own childhood. Self-compassion is hugely important in navigating all the transformations you might go through as a new parent. Finding others that meet you with understanding and care is the first step in making sure you can meet yourself and your child in the same way. 

*The stories in this article are a combination of experiences of several clients; any identifying information has been changed.

title: Most Teens Care, So Why Don’t They Always Help?
summary:
A student notices a classmate eating lunch alone. Another sees a peer being excluded from a group chat. Someone knows a friend has been struggling but hesitates before reaching out. Why?

Most adults assume the challenge is getting young people to care. But after spending years studying adolescent compassion, I have come to believe that caring may not be the central problem.

Many adolescents care deeply.

The question is what happens next.

We often imagine compassion as a straightforward process: Notice suffering, feel concern, take action. Yet anyone who has worked with adolescents knows that the path is rarely so simple. Young people are navigating friendships, social hierarchies, identity development, and concerns about belonging, all while learning how to manage their own emotions. In these moments, compassion is not simply a feeling. It is a decision unfolding within a complex social world.

In our recent research developing the Youth Compassion Measure, an assessment of compassionate responding, we find that most adolescents recognize when a peer is struggling. What varies is whether that recognition translates into helping. Across hundreds of students, four factors consistently shape whether compassion becomes action: peer dynamics, social risk, emotional regulation, and intrinsic motivation.

Understanding these factors may help parents, educators, and youth-serving professionals better support compassionate action in young people.

1. Compassion has to survive peer dynamics

One of the clearest findings from our work is that adolescents were more likely to help when the person experiencing distress was someone they knew well.

At first glance, this may seem obvious. Most of us are more likely to check on a close friend than a stranger. Yet this finding points to a deeper truth about adolescence: Compassion unfolds within relationships.

During adolescence, friendships become central to daily life. Young people are figuring out who they are, where they belong, and how they fit into their social worlds. Relationships provide security, identity, and connection. Unsurprisingly, those same relationships shape compassionate responding.

This means that compassion is not simply an individual trait. It is also social.

When educators talk about creating compassionate schools, they often focus on teaching empathy or kindness. Those efforts matter. But our findings suggest that fostering strong, supportive relationships may be just as important. Young people appear more willing to take compassionate action when they feel connected to the people around them.

In other words, belonging may do more than improve well-being. It may help create the conditions that allow compassion to flourish.

2. Compassion involves social risk

If relationships explain who adolescents help, social risk helps explain why they sometimes do not.

Consider a common scenario. A student witnesses a peer being teased. They know the behavior is hurtful. They may even want to intervene. Yet stepping forward could carry consequences. They may worry about being judged, excluded, or embarrassed, or becoming a target themselves.

Our findings suggest that adolescents are often weighing these possibilities, consciously or unconsciously, before deciding how to respond.

This is one reason public conversations about bullying can be so frustrating. When videos circulate online, attention quickly turns to the bystanders. Why didn’t anyone help?

The question assumes that recognizing suffering naturally leads to action. But social reality is more complicated.

Young people are often assessing multiple things at once: the seriousness of the situation, who is involved, who is watching, what might happen if they intervene, and what might happen if they do not. What appears from the outside as indifference may actually be a moment of conflict between compassion and self-protection.

This perspective does not excuse harmful behavior or passivity. But it does encourage us to understand helping as a social act rather than a purely moral one.

If we want young people to act compassionately, we need environments where compassionate action is socially supported instead of socially costly.

3. Compassion requires emotional regulation

Perhaps the most surprising finding from our study is that recognizing suffering alone did not consistently predict helping.

Many students understood that someone was struggling. The difference was what happened after that recognition occurred.

One of the strongest predictors of compassionate action is distress tolerance, the ability to remain engaged in the presence of emotional discomfort. This matters because witnessing another person’s suffering is often uncomfortable. We may feel sadness, anxiety, uncertainty, helplessness, or fear of saying the wrong thing. Adolescents experience these emotions, too.

Imagine a teenager whose friend is crying. The challenge is not simply recognizing that the friend is upset; it’s navigating the delicate space between overidentifying with another person’s suffering and distancing oneself from it. Too much emotional absorption can lead to overwhelm and withdrawal. Too much distance can lead to disengagement. Compassion requires something different: remaining connected to another person’s experience while maintaining enough emotional balance to respond effectively.

People sometimes assume that compassion and empathy are the same thing. They are not. Empathy allows us to resonate with another person’s experience. Compassion involves channeling that awareness into a desire to alleviate suffering. Doing so requires emotional regulation. Without it, concern can become overwhelm, uncertainty, or avoidance. Instead of moving toward suffering, we move away from it.

Our findings suggest that compassionate action depends not only on recognizing another person’s distress, but also on the ability to stay present with that distress without becoming consumed by it. In this sense, emotional regulation is not separate from compassion; it helps make compassion possible.

For parents and educators, this finding has important practical implications. Teaching young people how to navigate difficult emotions may strengthen their capacity for compassionate action. Skills such as mindfulness, emotional awareness, reflection, and distress tolerance are not simply tools for managing stress. They may also be the very capacities that help adolescents transform caring into action by staying engaged when helping feels uncertain, vulnerable, or emotionally difficult.

4. Compassion needs motivation

Even when adolescents care and have the emotional skills to stay engaged, one additional factor matters: motivation.

In our study, intrinsic prosocial motivation was one of the strongest predictors of helping. Simply put, adolescents who genuinely wanted to help others were more likely to translate concern into action.

This may sound self-evident, but it carries important implications.

Adults often try to encourage helping through external incentives, praise, rewards, or behavioral expectations. While these approaches can influence behavior, our findings suggest that compassionate action is especially powerful when it emerges from internal values and genuine concern for others.

Young people are constantly asking themselves what kind of person they want to be. When helping becomes connected to identity, meaning, and purpose, compassionate action appears more likely to follow.

This suggests that fostering compassion is about more than encouraging kind behavior. It is also about helping young people develop a sense of responsibility toward others and a meaningful connection to shared humanity.

What gets in the way of compassion?

Taken together, these findings challenge a common assumption.

There is a tendency to treat moments of inaction as moments of moral failure. We see a young person remain silent, fail to intervene, or walk past another person’s suffering, and we assume we understand what happened.

Yet our research suggests that these moments are often more complicated than they appear.

They unfold within social worlds shaped by belonging, friendship, identity, uncertainty, vulnerability, and the deeply human desire to remain connected to others. They are influenced by relationships, social risks, emotional capacities, and personal motivations.

What looks like indifference from a distance may sometimes reflect a struggle between compassion and the realities that make compassionate action difficult.

This perspective shifts the conversation from a question of character to a question of conditions.

Rather than asking whether adolescents are compassionate, we might ask: What conditions help compassion become action?

Helping caring become action

The encouraging message from this research is that the factors influencing compassionate action are not fixed traits.

Relationships can be strengthened.

School climates can be improved.

Emotional regulation skills can be taught.

Prosocial values can be nurtured.

When we think about compassion this way, the goal becomes larger than helping young people recognize suffering. The goal is helping them develop the capacities that allow caring to become action.

Perhaps this is what adolescence reveals so clearly. The distance between caring and acting is rarely empty space. It is filled with questions about belonging, uncertainty, responsibility, and risk.

Young people are learning to navigate that space every day.

Our responsibility as the adults who support them is not simply to teach them to care. It is to create the relationships, communities, and opportunities that help them act on the care they already possess.

title: The Surprising Connection Between Grief and Gratitude
summary:
Life as I knew it quietly began to unravel on a drizzly January morning in 2022. 

I was standing at the kitchen sink in a puffer jacket, staring out at my favorite persimmon tree, now bare. Only weeks before, the tree had been so full of persimmons that we collected them in huge plastic garbage cans for our neighbors to take by the grocery bagful. Our Labrador-ish mutt, Buster, was fat from persimmon overconsumption. 

Back then, the kitchen was loud, warm, and colorful. Our four kids were home for the holidays, bringing hungry friends and favorite songs, their late-night cookie-baking leaving sugar dust and dirty dishes everywhere.

Now that the kids were gone, my husband Mark and I conserved energy by leaving the downstairs heat off, telling each other we couldn’t justify heating the whole house just to keep the kitchen warm. We were real empty-nesters, ready to downsize.

Within weeks, we stripped our house of everything personal. We took down family photos, scraped butterfly stickers from hidden corners, and painted over the teal walls preteen girls had decorated. All traces of our family life vanished. We put our home on the market. It was the end of an era.

In December, my seemingly super-fit mom was diagnosed with ovarian cancer. Our house still hadn’t sold—by the time we put it on the market, mortgage rates had started climbing for the first time in two decades—but I moved into my childhood bedroom at my parents’ home to help my dad care for my mom. She passed away four months later.

A week before my mom’s memorial, I myself was diagnosed with invasive breast cancer. And a few days after my first cancer-related surgery, a close cousin died of an accidental overdose just after his 50th birthday.

Also during that time, a dear college friend, a fit, athletic doctor, had a fatal heart attack. And while I was having radiation for my breast cancer, our beloved dog Buster was diagnosed with lymphoma and needed to be put down.

Other losses were expected and even positive. Our house finally sold, and so we said goodbye to the home where we had  raised our four kids. I packed up that house through tears—for my mom, for my health, for my beloved dog and cousin and college friend, sobbing as I threw away things that marked my kids’ childhoods: boxes of ribbons from horse shows and swim meets, SAT score reports, so many old shoes and backpacks, homemade Harry Potter wands.

Mark and I put our stuff in storage and moved in with my dad for real while we renovated a new house in Berkeley. I loved this time with my dad; it made my cancer treatment and everything else bearable. He had always been my person, and now I got to cry and laugh with him every day, with no space between us.

About a year after my mom died, we finally moved into our new house. The first morning I woke up there and looked out the window at the whole Bay Area, I was astonished to see not one, but four rainbows touching down on the water of the San Francisco Bay. I felt welcomed and reassured that I was right where I was meant to be.

But then my brother-in-law Brian was diagnosed with a malignant brain tumor, the kind that doesn’t usually respond to chemo or radiation. They did everything anyway—brain surgery, chemotherapy, radiation, experimental drugs, an electromagnetic cap, expensive immunotherapy from Germany—but less than nine months later, he too passed away. I’ve never known a man with a bigger heart than Brian; when he died, we lost the emotional center on Mark’s side of the family. 

Our family was devastated. Again.

With each of these losses and life changes, I picked myself up and told my friends that at least it wasn’t my dad. When my dad dies, I’m going to stay in bed for a year, I said. When my dad dies, expect my complete collapse. I started believing that I could bear anything except for losing my father, my oldest and dearest friend. The loss of my father would leave a hole in my heart I knew I could never fill.

And then, in April of 2025, one month to the day after we lost Brian, my 84-year-old dad passed away. 

He was still driving, doing Pilates, and walking his dog Annie around his hilly neighborhood. He was still sharp as a tack, still hilarious, still going out every day to meet his many friends or his brother, Jud. He still volunteered and mentored others. 

One week, he was fully with us, bringing me a burrito for dinner at my nephew’s Little League game, taking us to dinner at the club where he’d been a lifelong member, buying tickets to a Giants game. The next week, he was gone.

My brother and I decided it “made sense” to sell our childhood home, a place that had anchored our extended family for nearly 50 years. But I could not make sense of how I could lose everything that centered me, my whole foundation, so fucking fast.

Still, I didn’t utterly collapse. I learned how to grieve in small moments throughout the day; how to keep putting one foot in front of the other while still feeling loss. I cried before and after work as I walked my dad’s sweet little Annie. I broke down at the grocery store, in restaurants, while hiking with friends, at the post office. I wept while packing up my parents’ house and while pulling apart their photo albums. I was exhausted, hollowed out. 

My heart was broken, but I got out of bed every morning.

I started new, truly energizing work projects and slogged through my parents’ stuff and another year of difficult firsts. The first Father’s Day without my dad, the first family birthday not celebrated at my parents’ house. As the first Thanksgiving without my dad and Brian approached, my therapist remarked that grief was often surprisingly life-enhancing. That was turning out to be true for me.

Thanksgiving has always been my favorite holiday. I usually host our big family, and I always have a lot to say at dinnertime about what I am grateful for. That year, the intimate connection between loss and gratitude had become painfully obvious to me.

Genuine gratitude—when we really pause to acknowledge how valuable something is—inherently involves recognizing the impermanence of that thing. True gratitude carries the awareness that what we’re grateful for won’t last forever; it’s here now but could be gone tomorrow. That awareness is what makes a moment feel more vivid and precious.

I think one gift of loss is that it can make us more intensely grateful. Not because we’re anxious about losing someone or something, but because we’ve learned viscerally that everything is temporary—and therefore extraordinary.

This crucible of loss and gratitude burned away my tolerance for anything that didn’t feel essential, helping me return to a deep spirituality. Standing at the edge of my own mortality and watching the structures of my life dissolve one by one fundamentally reordered my sense of what matters. Grief is the price of love, and it teaches us that love is what matters most.

So much loss has made pretense impossible for me. Grief strips us down and cracks us open, breaking down the defenses and distractions that keep us living on the surface. In the past few years, I’ve been to deep places, emotionally and existentially, that only truth can reach. I can’t un-know that now. Superficiality has started to feel like I’m being asked to forget the hard-won truth about how fragile and precious life actually is.

When we’re grieving, we can’t pretend. We can’t avoid our own vulnerability or the fact that everything ends. And while that’s devastating, it’s also strangely liberating. I feel more at peace, more permeable, more present, more profoundly loving, more alive to the texture of my lived experience. I’m attuned to what’s real and meaningful. I feel closer to and more in love with my friends and family than ever before. I feel things so deeply, and that depth is a kind of richness.

All of this is to say that growth happens in the broken-open places in our hearts. Loss and gratitude both dissolve the boundary between ourselves and the larger human experience. When we love and when we grieve, we join an ancient river of sorrow and love that connects us to everyone who has ever loved and lost.

I would never choose the losses I’ve endured. I’d give anything to have my people back, and not to have had cancer. But this is the grief-gratitude paradox: I also wouldn’t trade what grief has taught me, how deeply I feel, or who I am now because of all I’ve lost.

So this Thanksgiving, I’ll be at the table again, with fewer people than I’d like but more love than I ever knew I had room for. When it’s my turn to say what I’m grateful for, I won’t need to think about it. Every single moment is a gift. It’s all temporary, and it’s all extraordinary.
